extracted.intended_audience: literate general public / readers of The Spectator; those interested in manners, morals, and social character sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding criteria for depicting social types, virtues, and vices (men of pleasure, soldiers, youth vs age, women's men, modest tradeswomen) as argued in an 18th-century Spectator essay. Emphasises moral consequences, conversational tone, and behavioral detail useful for character sketches or moralizing essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure's corrosive effects on character
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure makes a man give up 'the Delicacy of his Passions to the Cravings of his Appetites' and causes him to lose perfect Joy for disappointing Gratifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and consequences: Pleasure approaches with 'warm Wishes, gay Looks, and graceful Motion' but leaves 'Disorder, Impotence, down-cast Shame, and conscious Imperfection.' Use vivid contrast between allure and aftermath; show how habitual pursuit of pleasure makes youth 'inglorious' and age 'shameful.' Anti-pattern: treating pleasure as unalloyed good or only an occasion for light comic episodes without moral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man of Wit and Pleasure — social/financial negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: In all Orders of Men where wit and pleasure are chief characters, the person is a 'negligent Friend, Father, and Husband,' and 'entails Poverty on his unhappy Descendants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray such characters leaving mortgages, diseases, and settlements as legacies; emphasize procrastination, irresolution and the practical costs of hedonism. Use concrete details (mortgages, settlements, Tyburn speeches) to show long-term harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure breeds irresolution and procrastination
rubrics_metrics.description: Irresolution and Procrastination in all a Man's Affairs are the natural Effects of being addicted to Pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict characters failing to act decisively in business or personal matters; link comic or charming surface behaviour to underlying incompetence. Scoring note: frequency and practical consequence of delay indicate severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent can mask vice — allure of gifted pleasure-seekers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some men of great Talents who sacrificed themselves to pleasure caused the pursuit to be received with quarter because 'The shining Qualities of such People have given a Beauty to whatever they were engaged in.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing vice, show how wit or genius can make it attractive to others; include examples where 'a Mixture of Wit has recommended Madness.' Anti-pattern: excusing vice because the character is talented without showing moral cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical courage in ordinary soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many in camps acquire a 'Mechanick Courage' from acting always in a Crowd: seeing many drop yet many more alive, observing narrow escapes and thus repeating dangerous acts without deep reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scenes of battle, distinguish between crowd-derived impulsive bravery and considered heroism. Show routinized indifference to death among the massed soldiery; avoid romanticizing their courage as noble without nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned, leaderly courage — resignation to greater good
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders are those 'who have reasoned themselves, out of a Consideration of greater Good than Length of Days, into such a Negligence of their Being' — they habitually put life at hazard for duty and glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray commanders who have consciously resigned personal preservation for service; emphasize motives (duty, glory, conscience) and the 'beauty' this reason gives to formerly ghastly dangers. Contrast with mechanical courage and show inspiring effects on subordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldiers' conversation: full of incidents, irregular but warm
rubrics_metrics.description: Military men's conversation is 'so full of Incidents' and has 'a certain irregular Way... which has something more warm and pleasing' than methodized discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing dialogue for soldiers, prefer anecdotal, incident-rich, slightly unstructured speech that conveys experience and frankness. Use vivid short narrations and allow conversational irregularity to signal authenticity and warmth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fellowship of danger produces mutual love and honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the fine gentleman-soldiers, 'Mutual Love is the Order of the Files,' officers are friends, private men are brethren; the commander is beloved and just in distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show reciprocal affection and moral exemplarity in leadership: fair pay, modest personal habits, visible concern for men's welfare. Use small gestures (refusing to wear lace, not taking more than pay) to signal honour. Anti-pattern: depicting heroic leaders as rapacious or indifferent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indifference and insensitivity caused by constant action
rubrics_metrics.description: Those habituated to constant busyness and pleasures become 'void of Thought' and indifferent to others' sufferings — 'the Devastation of Countries... are ordinary Objects' to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who, through continual excitement, lose compassion and complexity; use laconic reactions (e.g., 'he had a mad Horse') to illustrate emotional bluntness. Contrast with characters who retain sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age vs Youth — absurdity of wishing to be younger
rubrics_metrics.description: Wishing to be younger is 'unworthy a Gentleman'; the desire often arises from shameful past actions or vain longing for physical strength — both are contrary to Reason and Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portrayals of ageing, emphasize dignity, accrued capacity for rational pleasures (fame, contemplation, respectful commerce). Use aphorisms (e.g., 'He that would be long an old Man, must begin early to be one') to show cultivated acceptance. Anti-pattern: sentimental yearning for youth as inherently admirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old age enlarges rational pleasures and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The latter part of life enlarges capacities for 'the Conscience of a good Fame, the Contemplation of another Life, the Respect and Commerce of honest Men' and carries an authority preferable to youthful pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict virtues of old age: calm, reflection, social authority. Contrast with licentious youth described as feverish dreams; show memory of a well-spent youth as 'peaceable, unmixed, and elegant Pleasure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The social mechanics of female approval — how to be 'well with the Ladies'
rubrics_metrics.description: To be well with ladies one must cultivate 'A good Air at entring into a Room, a proper Audacity in expressing himself with Gaiety and Gracefulness' and adopt the conversation and deportment that women prize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For character creation, show social performers learning manner, audacity, and graceful talk; emphasize presentation and light affect rather than deep moral qualities. Scoring: success judged by ease of acceptance into fashionable female circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immodest impudence wins women of fortune; modesty can be penalized
rubrics_metrics.description: A sober modest man is 'looked upon... as a precise unfashioned Fellow of no Life or Spirit'; loosest principles and abandoned behaviour carry all before them in pretensions to women of fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting romantic plots, be aware that social reward may favor boldness and impudence over steady virtue; use this tension to create conflict. Anti-pattern: assuming virtue is automatically socially rewarded in courtship scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to portray a 'Woman's Man' (the successful gallant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Woman's Man is 'in his Air and Behaviour quite different': loose, negligent garb, soft and indolent manner, imitates the creature he hopes to betray, 'very knowing in all that passes from one Family to another', with 'little pretty Officiousnesses' and sometimes a bottle of spirits in his pocket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use costume and manner (careless dress, soft voice, petty offices) to signal a character designed to captivate women; include small, serviceable acts and family knowledge as calculated attentions. Show his reputation (being well with other women) as part of his currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modest tradeswomen suffer impertinent public discourse; call for deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Women who must work in public are subject to 'unreasonable Liberty' of immodest discourse; shop assistants and milliners face ribaldry that harms business and credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent public female workers enduring male impertinence; highlight economic consequences (losing customers) and advocate for male deference as a mark of honour. Use letters/first-person complaint tone to dramatize grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity among women often depends on singularity rather than sense
rubrics_metrics.description: A general favourite among women is rarely a man of good understanding; 'some Singularity in his Behaviour, some Whim... has recommended him to the other Sex.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When showing popular beaux, emphasize quirks, affectations, and performative oddities (quarrelling, dressing unlike the world, insipid assiduity) rather than genuine intelligence. This explains why an insincere yet witty rogue may succeed.
